summary: Adding and subtracting fractions with the same denominator within one whole (e.g. 5/7 + 1/7 = 6/7, 6/8 − 3/8 = 3/8). The core idea: the denominator NAMES the unit being counted (sevenths, eighths) and stays fixed, while the numerators COUNT how many of that unit and are combined like whole numbers — 'two fifths and two fifths make four fifths' just as two apples and two apples make four apples, where the 'apple' is the fifth. Teaching targets two misconceptions: adding the denominators too (2/5 + 2/5 → 4/10) and dropping the unit to give a bare whole number (6/8 − 3/8 → 3). For ages 7–8.
misconceptions: Adds (or subtracts) the denominators as well as the numerators: 2/5 + 2/5 = 4/10, misapplying whole-number addition (IES; ~10% of lower-achieving Y6 on an easy same-denominator item, NFER).
Drops the unit and answers a bare whole number: 6/8 − 3/8 = 3, operating only on the numerators as if the denominator weren't there.
Treats the denominator as a quantity to be operated on rather than the name of the unit being counted.

activities.title: Locked-unit bar combiner (fixed-denominator model)
steps: Work with a bar already partitioned into a fixed unit, e.g. fifths, with the label 'fifths' shown on the bar.
Combine 2/5 and another 2/5 by placing the pieces onto the bar; watch a running count read '4/5' as each piece is read aloud as 'one fifth'.

Test the answer '4/10' by laying four tenth-sized pieces next to the 4/5 you built. Notice that they cover only as much as two fifths, which is less than the four fifths on the bar, so 4/10 is the wrong amount. The pieces you are counting are all fifths.
Switch to subtraction on an eighths bar and remove pieces: start with 6/8 and take away 3/8, reading off 3/8 left.
Try adding one 2/5 too many and watch it run past the end of the bar, foreshadowing sums beyond one whole.
activities.insight: When denominators are the same, you are counting same-size pieces, so only the count (numerator) changes and the unit (denominator) stays fixed.

activities.title: Dual naming — read fractions as repeated unit fractions
steps: Say each fraction two ways: 'three one-fifths' alongside '3/5', and 'one one-fifth' alongside '1/5'.
State the sum both ways: 'three one-fifths and one one-fifth make four one-fifths' alongside '3/5 + 1/5 = 4/5'.
Do the same for subtraction: 'six one-eighths take away three one-eighths leaves three one-eighths', alongside '6/8 − 3/8 = 3/8'.
Point to the denominator each time and name it as the unit being counted.
activities.insight: A non-unit fraction is a repeated sum of unit fractions, so adding/subtracting is counting those units up or down — the denominator is the label, not a quantity to operate on.

activities.title: Number line counting in the unit fraction
steps: Mark a number line in the unit fraction (e.g. eighths) from 0 to 1.
For 6/8 − 3/8, land on 6/8, count back 3 eighths, and read where you stop (3/8).
For a sum, start at one fraction and count on in the unit, reading each step.
State whether the answer is bigger or smaller than one of the pieces and check your result against that expectation.
activities.insight: Fractions are quantities/points measured in the unit; combining them is counting on or back in that unit, and the answer is still a count of eighths (6/8 − 3/8 = 3/8, not 3).

activities.title: Paper strip folded/cut into equal parts
steps: Fold and cut a paper strip into the fixed unit, e.g. sevenths (or eighths), so every piece is the same size.
Build 5/7 + 1/7 by gathering pieces and counting them: six sevenths, 6/7.
Build 6/8 − 3/8 by setting out six eighth-pieces and removing three, leaving 3/8.
Say aloud what each piece is called and how many there are after combining or removing.
activities.insight: Physically counting identical cut parts makes clear that combining fractions of the same denominator is counting like units; the piece size (unit) never changes.

activities.title: Fluency practice and error-baiting check (companion)
steps: Complete fill-in items such as '2/5 + 2/5 = _/_' and '6/8 − 3/8 = _/_'.
Choose the correct answer to 3/8 + 2/8 from options that include 5/16 (add-across error) and 5 (bare whole number) as distractors, and say why each wrong option is wrong.
Shade pieces on a strip to match each sum or difference.
activities.insight: Same-denominator sums and differences can be rehearsed to fluency, and deliberately including the add-across and dropped-unit answers as distractors checks whether the unit idea is secure.

checkQuestion: Here are two to work out — show me each step as you go, out loud or on paper: 2/5 + 2/5, and 6/8 − 3/8.
checkAnswer: 2/5 + 2/5 = 4/5 (denominator stays fifths, add the counts 2 + 2). 6/8 − 3/8 = 3/8 (denominator stays eighths, 6 − 3 = 3).
